extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, patent practitioners, and respondents/participants in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED, ALJs, and counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, definitions, burdens, and sanctioning criteria applied in USPTO disciplinary proceedings addressing unauthorized practice of patent law and related conduct before the Office. Useful for evaluating practitioner conduct, defenses, and sanctions under USPTO rules and 35 U.S.C. § 32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49). Thereafter, Respondent has the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt; it requires evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations.' Cases cited (Addington v. Texas; Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler; Foster v. Allied Signal) explain 'clear' as certain/unambiguous and 'convincing' as reasonable/persuasive. The OED must meet this standard for each alleged violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office'
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office covers 'law-related service that comprehends any matter connected with the presentation to the Office or any of its officers or employees relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under the laws or regulations administered by the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b) and § 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples include preparing necessary documents in contemplation of filing with the Office, corresponding and communicating with the Office, representing a client through documents or at interviews/hearings/meetings, and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office. Proceedings before the Office include applications for patent, corrections of a patent, trademark registrations, appeals, petitions, or any other matter pending before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts constituting practice in patent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes, but is not limited to: preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish patentability; and drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law and the decision interpret these activities as practicing law (In re Amalgamated Dev. Co.; In re Herren; Kennedy v. Bar Ass'n). Mere transcription of a client's words may not be practice, but translating/rephrasing client statements into legal/technical language, drafting claims, and drafting responses with legal argument do constitute practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner status and applicability of USPTO disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who engages in 'practice before the Office' is treated as a 'practitioner' under the USPTO disciplinary rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.1; definition cross-referenced to § 11.14 and § 11.6). The Rules of Professional Conduct apply to persons who practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not registered for patent practice, an individual may be a practitioner for disciplinary purposes if they engage in practice before the Office in trademark or other non-patent matters; thus USPTO disciplinary authority can extend to unregistered persons who meet the definition by their conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice prohibited (only registered may prosecute others' patent cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only practitioners who are registered under § 11.6 are permitted to prosecute patent applications of others before the Office or represent others in any proceedings before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.10). Engaging in patent practice for others without registration violates the prohibition on unauthorized practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule applies irrespective of whether the unregistered person appears as attorney-of-record; the conduct (drafting applications, responses, advising strategy) itself is unauthorized. The USPTO considers itself a 'jurisdiction' for purposes of the unauthorized-practice rules. Recognition to practice trademark does not authorize unauthorized practice of patent law or practice in another jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false or misleading communications about services
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not make false or misleading communications regarding their services (37 C.F.R. § 11.701).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding oneself out as registered or able to provide patent legal services before the Office when not authorized falls within this prohibition. The OED may allege violations where practitioners misrepresent status or qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing or failing to fully respond to lawful Requests for Information (RFIs) from OED can constitute misconduct and undermine the disciplinary process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of privilege must be supported (e.g., privilege logs). Simply asserting lack of jurisdiction or privilege without producing requested documentation is insufficient; non-response or incomplete responses weigh against the respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to consider when imposing sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions, the Court must consider four factors per 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b): (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors guide the severity of sanction (suspension or exclusion). The decision applies the factors to weigh misconduct, intent (or negligence), injury (actual/potential), and aggravation/mitigation in choosing a sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's receipt of fees for unauthorized services, repeated conduct over years, and seniority/experience increase sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include the absence of a prior disciplinary record, evidence of good faith or that actions were well-intentioned, and remediation efforts (e.g., refunding fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such factors may temper the severity of sanctions even when violations occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual or potential injury affects sanction severity
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct is a factor in determining sanctions (part of § 11.54(b)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of evidence of actual or potential harm to clients weighs toward a less severe sanction; however, lack of injury does not preclude discipline if duties were violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies and procedural outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the USPTO under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and implementing regulations. Respondents may be suspended (the decision here orders suspension of not less than 18 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents have appeal rights: appeal to the USPTO Director within 30 days (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a)). Duties while suspended are set out in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; reinstatement requires petition under § 11.60(c). Constitutional challenges are reserved for appropriate forums after administrative remedies are exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process protections in disciplinary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary action under 35 U.S.C. § 32 requires 'notice and opportunity for a hearing.' Proceedings are conducted under USPTO procedural rules and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 556).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process is satisfied by reasonable notice of charges, opportunity to be heard, to present evidence, to cross-examine witnesses, and to participate in hearings. Constitutional challenges to procedure are typically deferred until after administrative proceedings conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required to show respondent misled clients about registration
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that a respondent misled clients into believing he was registered before the Office requires clear and convincing evidence; client assumptions or referrals alone are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony that a client 'assumed' the practitioner was registered does not meet the clear and convincing standard unless there is affirmative evidence that the respondent or others expressly held themselves out as registered. The decision distinguishes between clients' reasonable assumptions and actual misleading statements/conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege assertions in investigations must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent claims attorney-client privilege in response to OED RFIs, the claim must be accompanied by a privilege log or other supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide a privilege log or adequate support for privilege assertions undermines the claim and supports OED's position that the respondent did not fully comply with the investigation.
